items.title: How tape changed composition
items.claim: Magnetic tape recording became widely available in the late 1940s. Which composer used it to develop musique concrete in 1948?
items.reveal_title: Schaeffer's Etude aux chemins de fer, 1948
items.reveal:
Schaeffer used recorded train sounds to compose at RTF, Paris. The studio later became GRM (Groupe de Recherches Musicales).

The method established sound itself, separated from its source, as compositional material.
items.why: Recording media are not just preservation tools; they create new compositional possibilities.

items.title: What 'Well-Tempered' meant
items.claim: J.S. Bach's The Well-Tempered Clavier (1722, 1742) covers all 24 major and minor keys. Was Bach writing for equal temperament?

options.text: Probably a well temperament (such as Werckmeister or Kirnberger) where all keys were usable but each had different colour

items.reveal:
Scholarship suggests Bach used a well temperament such as those proposed by Werckmeister, where each key sounded subtly distinct.

Lehman's 2005 proposal even reads the cover ornament as encoding a specific tuning.
items.why: Historical performance research recovers sounds standard recordings obscure.

items.title: Equal temperament's compromise
items.claim: 12-tone equal temperament (12-TET) makes all keys playable. What does it sacrifice compared to just intonation?

options.text: All intervals except the octave are slightly out of tune relative to pure ratios
It only works for one key

items.reveal_title: Every interval except the octave is mistuned
items.reveal:
12-TET divides the octave into 12 equal semitones of 100 cents each. The perfect fifth is about 2 cents flat from the pure 3:2 ratio; the major third is around 14 cents sharp from 5:4.

Most Western fixed-pitch instruments since the 19th century use it.
items.why: A practical standard often involves giving up purity for portability across keys.
